TakeWalker:

 

lynkfox wrote:
I am -not- looking to be most effective in an RPG. I'm looking to tell a story, and a lot of a good story will be NOT being effective  
I think reactions to this system come down along this line. Are you willing to get into the spirit of the system and tell a story, or do you just care about winning, taking as few losses as possible? If the latter, this may not be the RPG for you. (Which, y'know, is hard to hear if you really like Sentinels and wanted to be able to enjoy it.)Speaking as someone who tends to eschew heavy roleplaying in RPGs for the cry of "Battle! XP! Loooot!", I feel like this system is a challenge that I want to rise up to. Yeah, let's go write a story, with all its ups and downs and twists and turns. I think it's because -- and this is entirely due to the first run of Sentinel Comics Live -- there's a sense that character actions matter, and matter in ways that only player actions matter in other systems.Like, of course my bard is going to cast Detect Magic and grab the ancient urn, heedless of the repercussions, because I want the cool, shiny, magic thing and who cares if there's a curse or a bad guy we'll need to fight because of it. I want more things to fight, it's more XP! Actions like that are things I've done constantly in games like D&D, where backstory is just a thing you write down for some bonus XP at the start of the game, refer to once or twice to let people know what your character is like, then completely ignore for the rest of the game.

 

I am in COMPLETE agreement with this. Remember, I said I am a compelte, unabashed, accomplished, Twink. I can break a system faster than you can count to 5 most days once ive gotten a chance to dig into it, and do it with starting XP on a few of them. I know what fun the crunchy, xp driven, loot based kill fest can be. In my heart of hearts however, I am a Story driven player. And thats what has me so excited for this system, especially after watching Christopher run it - it can be -very- story driven.

 

 

 

Jay Green:

I think reactions to MindWanderers criticisms are a bit misplaced.  These don't strike me as him wanting to have a crunchy combat fest.  They strike me as wanting clear, unambigouus rules.  If you don't think its possible to do this and also have an abstract, story focused game, you are wrong.  You just are, thats all there is to it.  Go play the Smallville RPG, which is also designed by Cam Banks, to see an example of exactly that. I think it is possible to have a different impression than MindWanderer without misplacing his motives.  If he says he wants chunchy combat focused gameplay, I'd say its fair to tell him he's looking in the wrong place.  But I think he is criticizing the game for having tactics focused elements and using those elements poorly, not for lacking those elements entirely.

 

Oh I certainly don't think its not possible! You can certainly have clear concise rules in a story driven game. I don't find the rules non clear or concise however, but I am also of the experience where more 'open' rules that allow the GM to do their thing and rely on the GM to make the best game possble are great rules and really the best thing for an RPG - writers aren't going to know players styles. GMs are. Giving a good, open framework for GMs to have a base common ground with their players to work in, and then making it open enough for GMs to mess with as needed to tailor the experience is the -best- kind of RPG in my opnion. 

Concerns about how fluid the Twists are just arent a concern to me. I -want- them to be fluid and open, so when I run a game I have more control over what happens rather than just consulting a chart and saying mmm ok. You take a -1 hinder or mmokay this villain gets a +1 boost. 

And yep, I totally said the other part of your post - He wants a more crunch game I totally get that. I don't think that the tactics elements in this game are very tactically myself, but thats a matter of opinion. I certainly don't have any real -criticsim- of his conerns, only that I don't necessarily see the system/game from the same angle. Not dismissing them, just trying to see if my explaining my view can give any insight to him or others reading.

 

XtremeGuardian:

I have found the best options is to not introduce the tracker until after the scene has been going for a few rounds and the villains/environment take specific actions to initiate the need for the tracker and impending doom. 

 

This is excellent Idea XtremeGuardian. And I believe its somethign that Christopher did several times - the scene tracker only came out when he -wanted- to put a sense of rush/time management/hurryness on them. They had many scenes without it at all (Such as the grimloid battle when they first arrived at the castle) - no reason to hurry them along there, let them take their time and do their thing.

 

XtremeGuardian:

Initiative: This is a huge concern for me as it actively fights certain play styles, buffs, and overcomes. As noted, there is no benefit to not try and have heroes all go and then villains, the problem is that this can give villains a big advantage in how things play out. For example, if somone uses a boot or buff like galvanize, pick him to start the next round and end his boost early. I find it needlessly random. My favorite solution to this was done in Feng Shui with the shot tracker. Players were put on the track based on a base speed roll and the level of their actions determined how large of a move they made down the track. Act in a lot of small actions or set up one large slow action. It also gives visibility to the order of character turns to set up better combos and strategies.

 

Totally see where you are coming from in this, and if it were a competitve game it would totally be a HUGE issue. As it is, I think it would be up to the GM NOT to pass it to legacy. Let the Boost stay a bit, its OK. You're not here to beat the players, you're here to tell a great story. You have that choice.

That being said, not every group sees their GM/DM/Storyteller to Players relationship as cooperative. They see it as antagonistic, and then what you describe is totally going to happen. That however is going to be a problem no matter what, because this system is clearly designed with the cooperative relationship in mind, as thats how Adam and Christopher see RPGs. - As such, there are going to be a ton of issues where if you have an antagonistic relationship between GM and Players, this system is going to break down fast.

 

XtremeGuardian:

 Advancement/Progression: I feel something needs to be done here. I love storytelling, but I feel there still needs to be a carrot to entice players to pursue buildign their character. This happens in comics too as charcters build new tech, learn a new way to use their powers, and discover crazy artefacts. My current thoughts are to introduce permanent buffs in the way of items that can be destroyed as major twists: such as Absolute Zero installing new focus points on his suit to give him a persisten +1 to cold rolls but that can be damaged or even destroyed as a major twist or sacrifice. This at least makes players feel that their character has the opportunity to evolve or advance in meaningful ways but cannot become overpowered over time. My thoughts.

 

I think its still posisble to evolve without direct progression like XP or such. However, I will freely admit that such things are much harder to show and feel. I admit to being a bit warry - because I have often found myself bored with video games that give to much or characters that start off with too much XP (because we wanted to play a high power game) as opposed to those same situations where I earned all those things from scratch. 

I don't know how this would fly with a regular group until I got it at the table. My feeling would be this would be a pause game, played for a sesson or 3 between another major campaign chapters, picked back up whenever you need a break from your hardcore DnD campaign or something.

 

 

 

Too all - Thank you thank you for participating. This is great discussion! I hope to keep it up.

posts.name: MindWanderer
posts.cooked:
So here's my opinion on RPG's in general: The rules matter.

If you want a game that's basically freeform storytelling, you can use FATE, you can use Amber, you can use No Thank You, Evil.  Or you could use D&D, or GURPS, or anything else you want.  It doesn't make any difference.  You don't need rules that stand up to any scrutiny whatsoever.  You don't even really need a game system at all.  You're just talking and telling stories, and the GM handles things however they feel like.

What would make you choose one game system over another is how they handle mechanically.  And then you get into what rules are balanced, consistent, and smooth.  When one character is more effective than another (when it comes to mechanical/dice-based challenges), that's a strike against the system.  When a player can approach similar problems in similar ways and make similar rolls, yet get drastically different results, that's a strike.  When the rules are hard to remember, hard to execute, or require frequent lookups on a table or flipping through a book, that's a strike.

A good GM can work around even the worst rules to create a fun game.  Sometimes that involves making house rules, sometimes it's filling in ambiguities, sometimes it's avoiding parts of the system that are the most janky.  Christopher did that himself; Sir Arton had an ability that was unfun, so he stopped using it.  That's an example of having a positive experience in spite of the system rather than because of it.  Same thing with initiative: early on, Christopher was expecting a crunchier gameplay style, so when the players screwed up the initiative order, he punished them by advancing the scene tracker 4 spots at at once.  The more sessions that passed, the more he realized that they were never going to be careful tacticians, and the less he punished them for bad decisions.

The reason I bring up Overcome checks as a concern is because of how they're integrated into combat scenes.  In most other games I've played, noncombat abilities can be used or not used in a much more freeform way.  Need to find a piece of information?  You could roll dice to get the word on the street or hit up a library, but you could also role-play talking to people, or pay someone off, or use magic.  When you're in a timed scene and you see a checkbox with "rescue the civilians" next to it, you look at your Principles, Powers, and Qualities, and think up a way to justify applying them to a single roll.  It's not a bad approach, but to me it makes every challenge feel the same.  You also have the "when all you have is a hammer, every problem looks like a nail" thing going on.

So on leveling up I have found that giving someone a static +1 is a bit much. Makes some things interesting. And uping a dice value up one is not too bad but can't do it too often otherwise you end up an all 12 character.

 

The best way to "level up" I found was to give ingame truth about the characters.
-A player got a lackey that was use to help and film the Character if it was put into harms way the person could die. 

-A player changed the name of their unique Quality form Model ->actor -> Minor celebrity (and Swag but we never made it that far.)

- All the heroes gave up their Collection to get a base. They worked all session picking up pieces to make a base.

-My transforming Character used it to pick up a new form.

-Gave someone a d6 in a new skill they want to learn.

 

But in my group 30 (6x5) session takes a year so I don't have to worry too much. And by then maybe Dave will have more solid Ideas on how to work the game.

Something that has just occurred to me, but in place of individual levelling, how about party based levelling?

At the end of a trade, say, the party define a d6 quality that represents them as a team which can be used in place of one if their qualities. At the end of the next trade, they can upgrade this to a d8, and then d10, but no higher.

You could cap the number of team qualities easily and they could have team powers (following the qualities idea) to represent trademark, but shared, equipment.

posts.name: aramis
posts.cooked:
Having run two groups through the starter kit, I look forward to the corebook.

In re the tracker issue powerhound 2000 mentions - players CAN slow down the tracker. It's a standard option. One overcome stops it from progressing next environment turn. This makes it actually much easier with larger groups to slow the tracker.

I think limiting each side to 3 activiations in a row is a good thing; 2 is not really better,

Limiting the environment to end of turn isn't great - but limiting it to either end or when the players want it works rather well.

The adventures have some issues.

  • The dungeon crawl is unsatisfying; a map would be much easier to run.
    • Same with the reactor.
    • and the house
    Not a map as in move counters on, just one to give a reference.
  • Missing stats for potentially hostile major NPCs is a failing, as well. Most especially:
    • Tempest
    • Haka
  • Several key elements are described adequately only in scenes after the one they first appear in
    • Sekebots
    • spiderbots

It's almost too literal an adaptation of the boardgame. The Environment is a real strong element in most, but not all, scenes, and can be a problem if the players mistake it for the goal.

posts.name: PlatinumWarlock
posts.cooked:
While the possibility exists for the group to keep the scene tracker from progressing, there’s a problem:

On a general level, that’s not fun. And trading off “scene tracker duty”, even if well described, becomes a chore instead of a game. Instead of doing proactive, heroic feats or challenging villains, you’re effectively putting one hero on “crowd control”, which takes them out of the action. And any experienced GM will tell you, nothing frustrates players more than taking away their autonomy.

posts.name: MindWanderer
posts.cooked: Well, the optimal strategy would be to wait until the scene turns red, then start blocking it like mad.  Then you're only losing a couple of actions per scene.  That's not overly burdensome.  And if the scene does turn red, you really do want to stop it from progressing if at all possible.  In theory, no one should ever lose from the scene tracker, unless they get so hindered they can't even roll a 1 on their Overcome (or the scene tracker advances by some other means, which would be pretty cruel of the GM).

posts.name: lynkfox
posts.cooked:
Well, if I were a player, 'blocking' the environment wouldn't be 'eh. I want to stop the environment from advancing' it be

 

The building is falling down around us! Crap! I want to use my strength + my archetechtual knowledge to find the support beams and support the building! 

 

The player may not even realize that is what they are attempting to do, and the GM interprets their actions as attempting to stop the tracker.

 

or as a GM, if a player said 'Can we not slow that down in anyway?"  I'd explain 'Well the building is falling down. What are you going to do about that?" and ask them to come up with something using their powers.

 

That to me would not feel like being stuck on 'scene blocker' duty. You'd be  takin an active role in protecting the others from the environment and holding back whats happening.

 

 

 

I guess that all comes down to a style of play. You have some groups who are story inclined. They'll think of their actions and decide what powers/abilities/challenges best fit that desired story action afterward. Then youi have the mechanically inclined groups. They will look for the mechanics of how to do something, what they need to do first, and maybe only grudgingly look for a story reason afterwards. Most groups are of course a mix of these extremes, but the second type or a group that leans that way is going to have a lot less fun in this system overall I think.

posts.name: lynkfox
posts.cooked:
actually, the SCLive is a good example of this:

 

You have Rae - Rae thinks of the story first. Which is why most of her actions used the same power/qualities every time. Its because she isn't thinking of mechanics, she's thinking of what would be cool or look awesome and then uses the system in the easiset way to do that.

 

you have Adam. Adam definitley leans story first, but pushes a bit more into mechanics. He will look for whats cool, but has a deeper undersetanding of how the mechanics work so will pick what works well for the situation - after he's decided what the coolest option will be (Ie: flying into a laser dragons mouth)

 

You have Maggie: Maggie is pretty half and half. She doesn't have quite the knowledge of the mechanics that Adam does, but she goes more for picking her ability an then describing it as cool than the other way around.

 

And finally, Craig is a bit more mechanic oriented - he wanted to use his defense powers, and so he engineered situations to make them more effective. As the game wore on that cerrtainly fell back a bit, but he still looked far more at his abilities first and what they did, then crafted the story around that to fit his needs. He was the one who most often talked about initiative order and getting his defense buffs up.

 

 

 

I think of anyone, Adam gets the most out of this system - He gets to use the most in ways of cool powers, but also takes advantage quite often of the freeform style and openness of the way the game can be run.

 

Craig however, is next in getting the most out of it - and thats simply because he has a higher understanding of the mechanics than maggie or rae. However, what he wanted to do (take everyones damage for them) soon became somethign that fell by the wayside because the mechanics didn't completely help his goal.

 

Maggie is at a stable middle place, she got to be cool, but also unfortuantely some of actions didn't work the way she wanted them too.

 

However, while Rae's actions may have been limited mechanically to only a few abilities, she certainly /personally/ got a ton out of this sytstem, and was able to make even a very limited knowledge of how the system does something work for making her character cool and awesome without too much outside input. 

 

 

 

And that is my point of this rambling post. Those who take the story direction as their goal in how to play this system are getting a lot out of it, even if they aren't very RPG literate. And thats awesome - it is very very friendly to peoiple who've never played a RPG before. And inexperienced players can still pull what little they know about the system to feel completely awesome and badass. (Rae)

Players who are experienced, but like to drive story more than they worry about the mechanics are going to find a great amount of fun in this system too (Adam)

Players who are middle ground in experience and in crafting story are going to be just fine (Maggie)

And Players who would like to do more with mechanics than story are going to find that sometimes the mechanics break down. They aren't as deep or robust as some other systems. The GM may need to craft a situations where what this kind of player wants to do is more possible. (Craig however switched to a more story concious mode after some ofhis mechanical desires started coming apart - so he still was able to enjoy the play, just he switched gears to be more like Adam)

 

 

 

 

I feel like every post in this thread has been leading to this conclusion : If you are a story driven type of GM/Player, or new to RPGs in general but are willing to tell a story, this system is amazing. Its great. Its going to give you so many options and you can really go to town with being the most awesome superhero you can be.

 

If you are a more mechanically expeirenced and inclined player, who likes/wants things to always have the clear cut answers a good mechanical system can provide (and not rely on the GM adhoc 'ing a situation together to make it work) this system is going to fall flat unless you can concentrate more on the story than the mechanics.

 


Fair assesment?

What you’re suggesting makes sense and, regardless of mechanical elements, good GM technique can cover a number of flaws.

But the issue here is one of context.  If the scene tracker is meant to represent the building collapsing, the scenario that you’re describing makes sense.  But, if the scene tracker is meant to represent the villains achieving some goal or escaping, with the building as some form of twist or environmental challenge (which is what we’ve seen more of through the various live-plays and the extant scenarios), then supporting the building becomes more tangential.

The nature of this system seems to be such that it behooves both players and GM to be mechanically transparent.  Things like investigation or technical manipulation (such as disarming a bomb) are continually pulled out as Overcome actions, for instance.  However, on many occasions, it’s not been quite clear what it ‘means’ when the scene tracker runs out.  In a chase scene, for instance, the scene tracker might logically represent the villain getting away.  However, if a minor twist causes a nearby building to collapse, holding up that collapsing building shouldn’t stall the scene tracker in any meaningful way; rather, stopping to ‘help’ would likely advance it (as the villain gets further away from the heroes while they’re…being heroes).

It’s just a touch wonky, and is nowhere near as concerning to me as the initiative meta-game, but it’s still an issue that some GMs (especially new ones, brought to the game by the Sentinels IP, rather than through other rpgs) will likely struggle with.

posts.name: Jay Green
posts.cooked:
I've finished as much of the stream as I am going to get to, so might as well respond to the initial misgivings I had.  The stream at least gave me confidence that the game is not doing what the starter kit advertised, which is railroady metaplot.  It was nice to see an original adventure with original characters.  

Other than that, the rules seem pretty mediocre, and the game as a whole does not know what it wants to be.  It has a lot of cool ideas smashed together, but not in a coherent or thought out way.  The playstyle seems to heavily rely on GM sensibilities as to what should happen next, with the rules just used as creative ways to justify that happening.  This is identical to free form play, but with a lot more painful fumbling about added in because apparently thats what you are supposed to do in RPGS (this is sarcasm, I have played many RPGs where the designer had figured out that this is not true).  

I disagree pretty strongly with the idea that story focused gamers will like this game and mechanic focused gamers will be dissatisfied.  First of all, while even have all the mechanical crunchy bits in the game if you already know that they won't be fun to use?  All you are doing is providing false hope for those mechanics focused gamers, and creating annoying distractions for the players who don't care about the mechanics.  Secondly, story vs mechanics, as it is being used in the current discussion is a false dichotomy.  If I am focused on the story, I want the mechanics to back me up, even if I am not paying attention to them.  What actually happens in these kinds of systems is that story focused gamers have to let the GMs interpret their input before they get to see if their story focus matters in the way they want it to matter.  If its the GMs job to step in and ignore the mechanics when they get in the way of the story, thats just another way of saying that the GM drives the story and the players do not.  So story focused gamers get betrayed by the system.

I still have concerns about the Scene Tracker because there have been cases where there have major foes able to accelerate it in addition to its normal progression.  With that it seems things escalate too quickly at times without the players able to do much about it. During the first issue on the live playtest, I expected someone to suggest Rae to do just that when the Lazer Dragon started burrowing into the ground, using her powers to delay it’s progress and give them more time to deal with it.
